b: All this week to get us in the holiday spirit, I’m going to be featuring holiday work stories from readers … and then updates season will start next week!
To kick us off, here are 15 of my favorite stories you shared about potlucks and other food gatherings at work earlier this month.

A coworker was having a baby soon, and we held a little party for her before her parental leave. The cake that was ordered was one of those “put a bunch of cupcakes together and frost all the tops together into one shape” set-ups so that people could grab a cupcake and go back to their work as needed. Someone had the idea to request it in the shape of an elephant because babies like circus animals or something.
It came in the shape of an elephant head … Use your imagination.
The kicker is that “IT’S A BOY!” was frosted down the trunk.

We had a chocolate fountain that somehow got knocked off of its axis and chocolate started spraying around the lunchroom. One colleague bravely volunteered to go in, and he saved the day, but ended up covered in chocolate.

My company chose a fairly fancy hotel for our Christmas do. They seemed to have the impression that serving tiny, artfully arranged portions was a good thing and missed the fact that fancy restaurants that do that are usually serving more than three courses. All courses were teeny, and the meat eaters main was a small bit of turkey, a singular roast potato, a single small carrot etc. The vegetarian main was a square of potatoes and vegetables with a few leaves and a drizzle of sauce. If I had to estimate calories, I’d say 250 tops?

Given many of us had been drinking Prosecco for a while before the meal, this did not end well. My partnered I are both veggie and we had to be driven home by our colleagues about 11, and stop on the way so he could throw up. Whoops! We will not be using that venue again.

One of my first office jobs was as a temp receptionist for a local office in 2007. I was 20 years old and was taking a break after a bad first year at college, so I hadn’t had any internships or anything else to prepare me for how to behave in a professional environment. While the office could theoretically accommodate around 100 people, they had a robust work-from-home culture and usually had about 25-40 people on-site on a regular basis. On some Fridays and Mondays, it could be just a dozen people in this relatively large office suite.

I somehow got it into my head that it would be a good idea to organize MONTHLY potlucks. Each one had a theme. I would mass-email everybody in the office with a signup sheet and reminders. The only one I explicitly remember is the ice cream potluck we had over the summer, which also happened to be for my birthday. So many people brought ice cream and toppings that I ate ice cream every day for two weeks.

Looking back on it, the only people who usually participated were the managers and directors who had actual offices (as opposed to cubicles) who sat near my desk. I don’t know if they were humoring me or what, or why NOBODY TOLD ME that it was completely bananapants to have a potluck every month!!! I’d be so annoyed if this happened at my current workplace.

I just went to an office happy hour where the restaurant served boneless wings as appetizers. There were regular chicken wings as well as a vegetarian option (cauliflower). They were mixed together in one pile, much to everyone’s despair.

I worked at a university financial aid office out of college where the director’s admin had a chess clock on her desk. She ate her lunch at her desk and couldn’t close the door because her desk was in a vestibule in front of the director’s. Her solution to ensuring she had her full lunch time was to bop the chess clock if you came in to ask her something, pausing her lunch time, and to bop it back once she answered your question. Respect for the boundary declaration, Barb! But she took that tenacity to organizing office catered events as well.

We had catered BBQ and once we were all formed in a line waiting, Barb went one by one down the line to explain to us what size spoonful we were to grab to ensure there was enough food for everyone. She carried an example spoonful. When our director heard what was happening, she followed Barb down the line and whispered, “We have enough food, take what you want” to each person.
You can’t make a full lunch potluck of things people want to eat and have the theme be Eggsellent. I will not be elaborating more on this matter.

At a catered lunch at the holiday party, a new employee picked up a half-finished tray of food and used that as their plate – piling it high with salads and rolls and desserts in the empty part of the tray. They sat with the tray in their lap, hunched over, and ate without looking up or speaking to anyone else. They were a noisy eater too, so noisy that the office manager who organized this meeting told them to wait until the speakers were done. Instead, the employee stood up with their tray and left to go finish eating at their desk.

Updated to clarify: I’m talking about a metal catering tray, the kind left out on a buffet line for people to take. It was half-full of macaroni and cheese. The employee just picked the whole thing up off the buffet line, including the scoop, and was carrying that and putting everything else they wanted in the part people had already scooped out.

I work in the pharmacy department of a large healthcare system, and we had a holiday party potluck. The next day, over 90% of the pharmacy department was out of commission with some wild form of food poisoning that took us all out for at least 48 hours. The few pharmacists and technicians who either hadn’t made it to the party or had been fortunate enough to avoid whatever food got everyone ill had to scramble to cover our various inpatient and outpatient departments. We had to cancel or reschedule whatever wasn’t an emergency so the few survivors could handle the absolute essential inpatient coverage.

People were furious! There was a witch hunt to discover which food had taken us out, to the point that people were making spreadsheets and interviewing all party goers on which food they/their family had eaten and cross-reference it with those who had or hadn’t gotten ill. Thank goodness there were 2-3 offerings that could not be ruled out, so no one was ever outed as the culprit. We have stuck with non-potluck parties ever since.

After a long stretch of multiple all-hands-type projects all happening at once, our lone HR person announced that our next all staff meeting would include “a special lunch” to thank us for all of our hard work. The lunch consisted of a pile of plain, untoasted bagels (and no way to toast them), tubs of plain cream cheese, and a pile of bananas that looked about 10 minutes away from being ready to become banana bread. And pitchers of water. We were literally served bread and water as a “treat.”

Allegedly, at one of my workplaces, there was a catastrophically bad karaoke party. They had booked a private room that was attached to a restaurant, and apparently everything was bad. Coworkers stuck in a small, somewhat dirty room that was too loud to talk but also had nothing to do and nowhere else to go, bad food and no alcohol, watching the same few coworkers sing on repeat because no one else was willing. This was well before my time, but it left a mark because when I took over party planning, I had half a dozen coworkers come up to me and ask me to promise to never do karaoke again.

Years ago I worked for a tiny nonprofit that had a terrible executive director. We had a lunch meeting set up with potential donors. The ED decided she wanted a local restaurant to donate a catered lunch. She made a big production out of going around to places in town asking for free food. There were only four of us in this meeting. She ended up with three egg salad sandwiches, which she proudly presented in a stuffy room and nobody touched. I couldn’t get out of the meeting fast enough. We didn’t get any money from the donors.

Several years ago I worked with a bunch of well-meaning but very misguided people who made the worst amalgamation of poor party committee decisions they possibly could: not only were we all expected to contribute cash for the catered main dish, but also contribute a homemade side to compliment it. The committee assigned food categories by last names. Added context, the setting was a university division in a very large urban area, so most folks were having to figure out how to transport their assigned compulsory potluck dish on public transit.

The kicker? This all went down the day I returned to work after traveling halfway across the country for a family medical crisis and I didn’t know about it until I got to work that day. I, an earnest 20-something, rule-following Millennial go-getter, very (VERY) uncharacteristically had zero effs after dealing with in-crisis in-laws for two weeks. Apparently I became a legend when I arranged for Pizza Hut to deliver a stuffed crust Hawaiian pizza*, stomped in with it, plopped it on the buffet table, announced that I was “sick of this shit,” took two slices, and stomped back to my office. Reports were that the remainder was gone in 10 minutes, and witnessing my totally unhinged actions was cathartic for many.

*I legit like this controversial pie, but also it was the most passive aggressive choice and I did that on purpose. While I’d make different decisions today and it certainly wasn’t my finest hour, I can’t muster up any regret either.

My dad’s office used to have an office-wide potluck every summer. Prizes were awarded for the best dishes, you earned bragging rights for the year, etc. My dad, who doesn’t cook and had other things to do, would:

a) buy a bucket or two of Kentucky Fried Chicken
b) place said pieces of KFC on a foil-lined baking sheet
c) crack pepper and sprinkle some paprika and other spices over the top
d) put the chicken in the oven at an extremely low temperature for about 10 minutes.

Whenever people asked about his DIVINE chicken, my dad would say something like, “Oh, just whipped it together” or “It was all my wife!” (meaning, my mom picked up the chicken). I’m not sure if anyone ever realized he was dishing up KFC, but I believe he received some awards and honorable mentions over the years.

I recently went to pick up a catering order for Friendsgiving and they had King’s Hawaiian rolls on sale in the store and I said to my friend “I guess they don’t have cheap ass rolls here” and the cashier said “I LOVE THE CHEAP ASS ROLLS STORY.” I feel like it’s now a code to find other AAM readers.
